newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ dollar ends sharply higher, wall at US$0.7000.
newsitem.headline: NZ dollar ends sharply higher, wall at US$0.7000.

text.p: A short-covering post-election rally saw the New Zealand dollar spike sharply higher on Monday but dealers said the currency should struggle to convincingly exceed US$0.7000 while the major political parties reposition themselves.
Kiwi ended at US$0.6977/84, up strongly from US$0.6920 at the opening, having traded a gaping 0.6920-0.7003 range. The Trade-Weighted Index was also strong at 66.64.
"I think Mr Birch has summed it up when he said the market's reaction has been pretty mature," said one dealer.
Finance Minister Bill Birch earlier told Reuters: "I think the financial markets have responded in a mature way."
The positive reaction to the election spread across all domestic financial markets.
In the case of the Kiwi, dealers said they were surprised by the number of people who had gone into the election short.
But the prime driver of the rally seemed to be the declining support for the far-left Alliance party.
"In hindsight there was greater focus on the diminishing support for the very left of the political spectrum, in other words the Alliance Party," the dealer said.

"While on balance the polls proved to be pretty accurate, the financial markets have been pleasantly surprised by the weaker support for the Alliance and I guess the feeling is they will have a lesser part to play in terms of setting the economic policies going forward," he said.
The common view in the market was that a centre-left coalition comprising the Labour and New Zealand First parties would form, but the markets would get tetchy if the process dragged on for too long.

"While we have seen some significant gains on the day, we are not quite out of the woods just yet. The next two-to-three weeks will be very interesting, foremost to see just what coalition does crystallise as the one that's going to form the next government. Secondly, any changes that are communicated in terms of economic policies and how they are going to be implemented," the dealer said.
While the markets had undoubtedly taken a positive view of the election, few expected any kind of settled trading pattern while the coalition-building process took place.

"The market has certainly taken a positive leaning to what has transpired after the election but I don't believe that it's all going to be all one way. I think we'll see a pretty volatile currency and debt market over the next two or three weeks," he said.
Interest this session had come mostly from overseas, interspersed with sporadic activity from domestic and interbank players.
Consolidation is expected in the 0.6960-95 area for the time being, but with fairly solid resistance over 0.7000, where there had earlier been heavy selling.

"Now we've got the uncertainty as to which way (New Zealand First leader) Winston Peters is going to jump and how much the major parties have to give in to Winston to form a government," said one dealer.
He expected the currency to trade a 0.6930-0.7030 band until there was some clearer direction on the political front.
"The main feature now is what the two main parties are going to do now to get Winston. That's the real thing the market is focusing on and waiting to see," he said.
